# Offline dependency resolver

Run with Node.js 24 (no packages or network access):

```sh
node resolve.js --input catalog.json --out lock.json
node resolve.js --help
```

The input is strict JSON with exactly `packages` and `roots`. `packages` is an
array of `{name,versions}` and each version is `{version,dependencies}`; roots
and dependencies are `{name,min,max}`. Every nested object is checked, including
unused packages and versions. Names are nonempty literal strings (whitespace,
Unicode, and prototype-like names are not trimmed), versions and inclusive
bounds are integers 1..1000, and `min <= max`. Unknown fields, wrong types,
duplicate package/version/dependency/root identities, and malformed JSON are
rejected. An unknown referenced package is instead a valid unsatisfiable
candidate.

Resolution includes exactly the root-reachable closure, one version per
included package, and permits satisfiable cycles. The exact objective is global:
sort *all catalogue names* by JavaScript UTF-16 code-unit order, form the
complete version vector in that order with `0` for absent packages, compare
vectors lexicographically, and maximize it. This is not greedy root order and
not minimum package count. Output is UTF-8 JSON of exactly
`{"packages":[{"name":"...","version":1}]}`, sorted by name, with a final
newline. Empty roots therefore output `{"packages":[]}\n`.

Run offline on Node.js 24 with no dependencies or network:

```sh
node resolve.js --input catalog.json --out lock.json
node resolve.js --help
```

Exit status 0 means success, 2 means valid but unsatisfiable, and 1 means
malformed input, CLI error, or I/O failure. Successful publication uses a
same-directory temporary file, fsync, and atomic rename. Input/output direct,
symlink, and hardlink identity collisions are refused. Every refusal happens
before replacement, preserving input bytes and any existing output; repeated
valid inputs produce identical bytes.

Run the complete dependency-free test suite with:

```sh
npm test
```

This runs `test.js`, `test-impossible-cycle.js`, and `test-inline.js`;
the suites invoke the real CLI in subprocesses and include exhaustive
independent-oracle cases, refusal preservation, cycles, and fixture traps.

A real fixture example is `fixtures/greedy-trap.json`, whose roots request
A in [1,2] and B in [1,1]. A version 2 requires C2 while B requires C1, so
the resolver produces:

```json
{"packages":[{"name":"A","version":1},{"name":"B","version":1},{"name":"C","version":1}]}
```
